title: The shared tabular pipeline: a four-quadrant benchmark and ten public datasets
request: Turn the HyperAck experiments into one reusable pipeline, benchmark every model family safe vs unsafe and baseline vs optimized (including a tabular transformer), and replay the same ladder on ten public datasets.
spec: general_pipeline/ with one runner for every model and mode; a 44-run benchmark (11 models in four quadrants: safe or unsafe features, default or optimized settings) on HyperAck's locked split; a 140-run benchmark on ten UCI datasets (7 models, baseline and optimized); a per-dataset 15-step playbook ladder with notebooks and reports.
plan: Write general_pipeline/ so the HyperAck runner, the external runner and later the research package import one implementation.
Run the 4-way HyperAck benchmark: 11 architectures (boosting, forests, stacking, a soft vote, an FT-Transformer, linear models) in each quadrant.
Cache ten public UCI classification datasets under data/public/ and run 7 models with baseline and optimized settings on a stratified 80/20 split, subsampling tables above 20,000 rows.
Give each public dataset its own project folder with the 15-step ladder, a safe-vs-unsafe arm where a leak is known, notebooks and three reports.
Plot and tabulate the results under research/tabular-classification/evaluation/benchmark_outputs/.

decisions.decision: Run every architecture in all four quadrants on the identical split.
decisions.why: Holding the split fixed separates the effect of leakage from the effect of the model and of tuning.

decisions.decision: Keep the pipeline at the repository root rather than inside a research folder.
decisions.why: Other tracks and the dclab_rnd package import it, so it must work without installation.

decisions.decision: Use HyperAck's safe-tuned settings as the optimized arm on the public datasets.
decisions.why: The pipeline was meant to be reusable on future datasets with one recipe (general_pipeline/playbook/FUTURE_DATASET_PIPELINE.md).

change: New general_pipeline/ package (runner, models, benchmark plots, playbook with FeatureEngineer and run_playbook.py), results for the 44-run HyperAck benchmark and the 140-run public benchmark, ten external project folders and two master reports.

findings.defect: The public benchmark's best scores for two datasets include a column known only after the outcome.
findings.scenario: bank_marketing reached ROC-AUC 0.939 with call duration as an input, though duration is known only when the call ends; online_shoppers reached 0.932 with PageValues. The later evidence campaign measured their apparent lifts at +0.1842 and +0.1968 training-CV ROC-AUC and honest holdouts of 0.7718 and 0.7394.
findings.cause: The external runner had no prediction contract per dataset, so every column was used.
findings.fix: The playbook ladders carry a safe-vs-unsafe arm where the leak is known (bank duration, shoppers PageValues), and the evidence campaign blocks both columns by its decision-time contract.
findings.test: evidence/campaigns/model_building_50_v1 leakage audits EXP-007 and EXP-042.
findings.impact: Read as a leaderboard, the benchmark put bank_marketing at 0.939 and online_shoppers at 0.932. Without the leaky columns the honest holdouts were 0.7718 and 0.7394, so anyone sizing a decision on the benchmark would have expected far more than a deployable model gives.
findings.open: The 140-run results stay as recorded, with the leaky columns in them; only runs made under a decision-time contract are protected.

measurements.name: 4-way HyperAck benchmark
measurements.gate: Compare all 11 architectures on the same split in four quadrants; no pass threshold.
measurements.result: Safe optimized: LightGBM 0.9449, stacking 0.9445, CatBoost baseline 0.9435, FT-Transformer 0.9186 (0.9051 at defaults, the largest tuning lift, +0.0135), logistic regression 0.8818. Leakage lifted every family: boosting +0.034 to +0.041, FT-Transformer +0.046 (0.9186 to 0.9647).
measurements.next: Treat the transformer as not worth its cost on this table unless a later dataset says otherwise.
measurements.against_gate: There is no threshold. On the safe side, optimized LightGBM leads at 0.9449, with stacking at 0.9445 and the CatBoost baseline at 0.9435; the FT-Transformer reaches 0.9186 after the largest tuning lift, +0.0135 from 0.9051. Leakage lifts boosting by +0.034 to +0.041 and the FT-Transformer by +0.046, so the leak is of similar size for every family.
limits: Every quadrant uses the same single split; the gaps between the top models (0.9449, 0.9445, 0.9435) are smaller than one split can resolve.
Models are compared on the split they are reported on, so no number here is a held-out estimate of a chosen model.
The size of the leakage gap belongs to HyperAck's two final fares; other leaks behave differently.

measurements.name: public benchmark, 140 runs
measurements.gate: Best ROC-AUC per dataset across 7 models and two settings; no pass threshold.
measurements.result: adult 0.927, bank_marketing 0.939 (with duration), breast_cancer 0.999, credit_default 0.797, german_credit 0.811, heart_disease 0.962, mushroom 1.000, online_shoppers 0.932 (with PageValues), spambase 0.988, wine_quality 0.916.
measurements.next: Rerun the datasets through an evidence-first campaign with a contract, training-only selection and one holdout read.
measurements.against_gate: No threshold was set. The best scores run from credit_default's 0.797 to mushroom's 1.000, but bank_marketing's 0.939 includes duration and online_shoppers' 0.932 includes PageValues, so those two measure leaks, not models.
limits: The best model and setting is picked on the same split it is reported on, so each best score is optimistic.
Large tables were subsampled, so their scores describe a sample of the data.
The optimized arm reused HyperAck's tuned settings instead of tuning per dataset.
No dataset had a prediction contract, so nothing kept post-outcome columns out.

outcome: One pipeline every later campaign imports; the leakage gap measured across 11 architectures; ten public projects ready for the evidence campaign. The best-per-dataset table is a leaderboard, not evidence, until each dataset has a contract.
lessons: The leakage gap is about the same size for every model family, so changing the model never fixes a leak.
A benchmark without a prediction contract per dataset reports leaks as wins.
The playbook's derived features were later found to do arithmetic on category codes (see RD-category-codes); generic feature generation needs to know which columns are categories.
risks: Running the safe and leaky arms on different splits, so the leakage effect is mixed up with split noise.
A benchmark over many public datasets without a prediction contract per dataset, which reports leaks as wins.
Reading a best-of-many score on one split as an estimate of real performance.
Placing the pipeline where other tracks and dclab_rnd cannot import it without installation.
Generic feature generation that cannot tell category codes from quantities.
